newsitem.title: USA: Grant's Municipal Bond Observer - Nov 29.
newsitem.headline: Grant's Municipal Bond Observer - Nov 29.

text.p: It is symptomatic of the state of the municipal market that when we were looking for a "buy" for this edition, the best we could come up with, at least on a tax-exempt basis, were the BBB-minus bonds of an as-yet-unbuilt Florida bridge, the future of which is imperiled by an environmental lawsuit. We discuss this paragon of speculative beauty on page 2, yet here note that even an uninsured bond laden, at least for the moment, with judicial risk yields but 6.34% to its maturity in 30 years. This is how it is these days in the municipal market.

Tax-exempt interest rates are at their lowest levels in nine months. The Bond Buyer's 20-bond general obligation index, which measures the yields on 20 GO bonds due in 20 years, was at 5.55% when this issue went to press, and most market participants seem to believe that it is going to go still lower, absent some horrific and hitherto unimaginable event.
We called up a couple of the more thoughtful souls who always seem to have interesting investment ideas for those seeking to put money into the tax-exempt market. But we found- surprise - not a one.

Joe Deane, of Greenwich Street Advisors, is fully invested. In fact, he says that if he scraped together all the cash his funds have on hand, it would amount to, "oh, $1.35." He sees rates drifting even lower over the next six to eight weeks. "And there's nothing to stop the stock market, either," he said.

Not everyone on our list is fully invested in municipals. "I have 15% in cash," Ken Woods, of Asset Preservation Advisors in Atlanta, advised us. "Twenty percent," confided Mike Crofton, of Rittenhouse Trust. We suppose if they want it, there will be plenty of supply for these fellows to look at over the next few weeks, as smart issuers and their even smarter bankers rush to take advantage of the crumpling of the tax-exempt yield curve by selling refunding bonds.

Most of those we surveyed saw very little on the municipal market investment horizon. Crofton, though, ever the contrarian, told us, "Rates will probably bounce up once more, hiccup maybe 50 basis points, to 7% on the Treasury's long bond."

He offered his reasons. A "pretty decent" retail selling season "will lull people into believing that the economy has some steam left in it," he said. "Then the bills will come in, people will realize that they've got far too much in credit-card debt and the economy will shut down. The Fed will tighten sometime during the first quarter, of course, and into the slowdown, making the contraction even worse. Then you'll see yields of less than 6% on the long end." All in the first quarter? we asked him. "All in the first quarter," Crofton replied.
This is how it is in the municipal market right now. And we know, or think we know, what happens when tax-exempt rates get too low: Buyers don't buy.

What we are still trying rather desperately to comprehend, however, is what happens when the stock market rises, and rises, and rises. The Dow, at this writing, had 7,000 in its sights and was closing fast. They call it "momentum buying."

--Joe Mysak, Editor, 212-809-7994 (The opinion presented is that of the author. Reprinted with the permission of the Interest Rate Publishing Corporation. All rights reserved. Grant's Municipal Bond Obeserver, Vol. 3, No. 23, November 29, 1996. Copyright 1996.)
